articles.title_orig: NFL Week 3 Sunday aftermath: Tyler Loop's heroics, Drake Maye concerns, Brock Purdy's MVP form
articles.title_zh: NFL Week 3 Sunday aftermath: Tyler Loop's heroics, Drake Maye concerns, Brock Purdy's MVP form
articles.content_orig:
Week 3 was all about the nail-biter.
Of Sunday’s 14 games, 12 ended within one score, and most came down to the final play, including Matthew Stafford 's last-second interception to cement the Rams' second-half collapse at Denver in the nightcap.
Let’s run through key storylines in the aftermath of a Sunday that provided a plethora of heart palpitations, including:
But first, we head to Brazil, which hosted an early contender for Game of the Season on Sunday.
Football’s ability to inspire never ceases.
Ravens kicker Tyler Loop rode a rocky path during his rookie campaign, culminating in a season-ending miss in the team’s Week 18 loss to the rival Steelers with the AFC North title (and the accompanying playoff berth) on the line. That pushed 44-yard kick attempt set in motion an offseason of change in Baltimore. Loop fended off questions about his future, keeping his job despite the immense fallout.
A blocked attempt in Week 2’s disappointing loss to the Saints revived questions about the 2025 draft pick. Then, on Sunday in Rio de Janeiro, Loop got his shot to brush away the haze of the past.
After the Ravens' defense bowed up and kept Dallas out of the end zone late in the fourth quarter, seven seconds remained in 31-31 game. Lamar Jackson rocketed a missile that Zay Flowers leaped to snag for a 27-yard gain , with the receiver immediately getting down as Jackson called a timeout with 1 second remaining and the ball now at Dallas' 38-yard line. Loop lined up the 56-yard attempt and calmly banged it through, with CBS Sports' Jim Nantz eloquently calling the game-winning boot “a trio in Rio.”
Ravens players celebrated with their sometimes-maligned kicker as they pulled off a last-second victory despite stumbles along the way.
Loop’s kick on Sunday didn’t erase the previous big miss or guarantee anything about his future. However, it provided oxygen to a flickering flame. That one kick could have revived a career.
"I was saying on the sideline, 'Your legacy starting now,' because I feel like he has been facing adversity," Jackson said of Loop . "I said, 'What a way to start your legacy in Brazil,' and he finished the rest. He did it. Shout out to special teams, shout out to Loop."
Jackson’s part shouldn’t be understated, either. His ability to deliver that late laser over the middle -- without taking too much time -- was pivotal, as was Flowers' snag and haste to get down. The Ravens moved the ball well on Sunday, but they also were stuffed in short-yardage situations several times.
In a young season in Jesse Minter’s first campaign, the 34-31 win showed fortitude: from the defense keeping the Cowboys out of the end zone on their final drive to Jackson making a play to Loop nailing the winner. It’s the type of victory that could propel a team.
The Ravens needed the win in a hotly contested division.
The Steelers' offense showed life in a 30-27 victory over the Bengals, with Aaron Rodgers finally hitting on some deep strikes after two weeks of them falling incomplete. If the Pittsburgh offense can keep splashing plays, and Rodgers isn’t broken in half, the Steelers will be a tough out.
Cincinnati’s defense came back to the pack a bit after an excellent start to the season. That’s not too much of a surprise. That’s not why Cincy lost, however. Special teams issues were the real killer, as the punt crew gave the Steelers extra chances. Joe Burrow still had a shot late, but a final-drive fumble sealed it. It’s a stinging loss to a division rival, but not one that should worry Bengals fans.
The Browns' defense was locked in again to improve Cleveland to 2-1 , stymying Bryce Young and a Panthers offense that had moved the ball well in the first two weeks. Deshaun Watson showed that, when he avoids the big mistake, he can be a net positive for Cleveland and make game-winning plays. That’s new.
The Patriots were pegged to regress in 2026, partly because of their tougher schedule after winning the AFC East. That might be one element of New England's 1-2 start, but it’s far from the story.
The biggest issue isn’t that the Pats are facing teams that make them pay for mistakes; it’s that Drake Maye has regressed to the point that he’s making rookie-level blunders in Year 3. Week 1’s calamitous turnover fest in Seattle has snowballed. Maye has seven giveaways through the first three games of the season, the most by any player in the NFL. His seven turnovers are the most by a Patriots player in the team's first three games of a season over the last 30 years, per NFL Research.
Perhaps he can explain away the embarrassing fumble in Sunday's blowout loss to Jacksonville, saying there was blood on the ball from the center. But there was no excuse for his second-quarter interception in the end zone. It was a ball that should never have been thrown. That’s Maye’s biggest issue right now: He’s not seeing things clearly. Defenses studied his weaknesses all offseason, and he hasn’t adjusted. Until Maye does, more upchucks like Sunday's performance will ensue.
"I think quarterbacks want to make plays,” Vrabel said Monday morning on the Greg Hill Show, via ESPN's Mike Reiss . “I think they want to throw touchdowns. I think sometimes when Greg and I go golfing, we really want to make a good score, right? Sometimes we’re so focused on it, we try to choke the life out of the golf club, and we’re squeezing it so damn tight that the ball has no choice but to go sideways.
"We need to stop trying to choke the life out of every single play. We need to relax. We need to settle in and go play football and not try to force things that aren’t there.”
Gregg Rosenthal, Jourdan Rodrigue and Nick Shook recap the Week 3 matchup between the Raiders and the Saints.
I already noted last week that the way Las Vegas has been winning is different under Klint Kubiak. It feels repeatable.
The defense has been opportunistic, taking advantage of turnovers. Las Vegas had four takeaways in the fourth quarter of its Week 3 win at New Orleans. The Raiders had only three fourth-quarter takeaways in the entire 2025 season, according to NFL Research. It’s also the first time a team has forced at least four fourth-quarter takeaways in a game since the Cowboys in Week 13 of 2022 vs. the Colts. Yes, the Raiders benefited from a controversial fumble call on Tyler Shough . It also takes players creating such opportunities to benefit from them.
Tight end Brock Bowers ’ return was pivotal. Vegas doesn’t win in NOLA without his 10-catch, 116-yard, one-TD performance. Kubiak deployed Bowers all over the formation, in-line and detached, making him a matchup nightmare. Despite Bowers missing the first two games after undergoing a knee procedure, a magical season for the TE appears quite viable, with Kirk Cousins force-feeding his top target. This offense needs one more outside option to be complete.
The Raiders are the darlings of the league right now, and rightfully so. Kubiak has quickly shown he can win in the big chair. His coordinators have been excellent. Cousins has been steady. Playmakers are making plays. But I should point out that the Raiders' opponents are a combined 1-8 through three weeks. The real test comes in next Sunday, when Kansas City visits Las Vegas .
“It’s a great f---ing win,” Raiders star defender Maxx Crosby said postgame in the locker room . "But we’ve got a great f---ing team coming into town. We already know what it is. It’s the f---ing Kansas City Chiefs.
“Enjoy this s--- tonight, take care of your bodies, and we’re f---ing on a warpath to get what we want, men.”
San Francisco 49ers fans should thank their stars for Brock Purdy and Christian McCaffrey -- and pray they don’t succumb to the injury bug that continues to plague the club.

Zoom in: That narrow overlap is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched Chinese officials this weekend on a "notification mechanism" for AI incidents with national-security implications.
Reality check: So far, nobody has publicly defined what would make the red phone ring.
Between the lines: Washington and Beijing already have crisis hotlines, as well as a history of going dark when they're needed most.
The bottom line: The very existence of the proposal is an acknowledgment that AI is no longer just another arena of U.S.-China competition. A serious failure on either side could quickly become a shared crisis.

Hello football friends, and welcome to the Monday edition of the Pick Six newsletter!

That was one of seven upsets that we saw in Week 3.
If you felt like every game on Sunday was close, you're not crazy. There were a total of 12 games decided by a single possession, which is tied for the most for any day in NFL history and the most for any week in league history. If we get a one-score game tonight, that will set the NFL record for most one-score games in a week, but don't count on that happening, because every Monday night game has been a blowout so far.
Anyway, it's Monday, so you probably already know what's coming your way: We've got grades from every game, plus some overreactions. And of course, we'll be breaking down the J.J. MCCARTHY TRADE that went down on Monday afternoon.
As always, here's your daily reminder to tell all your friends to sign up for the newsletter. To get them signed up, just click here .
For the first time ever, CBS got to air an international game and it ended up being possibly the craziest international game of all time with the Ravens beating the Cowboys in Rio De Janeiro. Maybe the NFL should put all their games in Rio.

If you want to see Carter's list of winners (and a couple of other losers), be sure to click here .
Everyone on the internet loves to overreact to things, and that's especially true when we're talking about the NFL. Personally, I overreact to everything. With that in mind, Zach Pereles decided to take a look at several things that happened during Week 3 to decide if we're all overreacting.

The Raiders can only play who is on their schedule, and their wins are now over the Chargers (who look miserable), the Dolphins (who might not win a game) and the Saints (who might be good but might be just OK). articles.title_orig: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow policy ending medical treatments for transgender inmates
articles.title_zh: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow policy ending medical treatments for transgender inmates
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Trump administration on Monday asked the Supreme Court to revive for now a Bureau of Prisons policy cutting off certain medical interventions and social accommodations for transgender inmates.
The Justice Department's emergency appeal stems from a federal district court order issued last month that continued to prohibit the Bureau of Prisons from enforcing its new rules against any inmate who is or will be diagnosed with gender dysphoria.
The judge overseeing a challenge to the policy, U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, ordered the Trump administration to continue providing medical care to a class of transgender inmates.
A group of inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria filed a lawsuit last year after President Trump issued an executive order at the start of his second term that prohibited the use of federal funds for medical procedures or treatments for transgender inmates within the federal Bureau of Prisons system. On the heels of that directive, the bureau issued new guidance that prohibited staff from granting requests for clothing accommodations for those inmates and barred the use of federal dollars for medical interventions.
The Bureau of Prisons then issued a new policy in February that it said was independent of Mr. Trump's executive order. Under those rules, the agency would continue providing mental health services for inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria, but would not provide surgeries, hormone therapy or social accommodations, like chest binders, wigs or breast padding, to address gender dysphoria.
Lamberth agreed to block the new rules in June and ordered the Bureau of Prisons to continue providing medical treatments to transgender inmates. The judge ruled in part that the administration's new policy was "reverse engineered" to implement Mr. Trump's executive order. He then issued an order last month continuing to block enforcement of the rules.
The Justice Department appealed. Earlier this month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit declined to restore the policy while proceedings moved forward.
In its request for emergency relief to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration accused the district court of "substituting its own policy judgment for that of the agency." The Bureau of Prisons, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said, determined its policy on medical treatments for transgender inmates was "necessary to maintain institutional security," and he warned that the district court's decision "nullifies" that judgment.
Sauer said the lower court order "prevents the application of the Executive's chosen policy" on a broad basis.

Yields on the longer end of the curve rose further to multidecade highs on Monday as a bond sell-off deepened.
The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ), often referred to as the most critical number in global finance for its widespread use as a benchmark rate, advanced roughly 5 basis points to 5.25%, its highest level since 2007, when yields rose in the run-up to the Great Financial Crisis.
Further out on the curve, 30-year Treasury yields ( ^TYX ) advanced by 6 basis points to 5.57%, a level not touched since 2004. The short end was also under pressure, as the 2-year yield ( 2YY=F ) rose by roughly 8 basis points to 4.93%.
Read more: How soaring Treasury yields could hit your finances
Bets on further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, an energy crisis kicked off by the war in Iran, ballooning US government debt and budget deficits, and a historic investment cycle driven by the AI build-out have all contributed to a sell-off that has spooked investors.
Of those concerns, the Federal Reserve is perhaps the biggest focus for investors. Earlier in September, the Fed issued a quarter-point rate hike, raising the US target lending rate for the first time in three years.
"We now have data broadly defined that says the economy has indeed strengthened," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press conference following the meeting. "Underlying growth is higher. Inflation is the problem. Stable prices have been the problem for now more than five and a half years."
More notable than the hike itself, however, were projections indicating that a majority of voting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) members expected at least another quarter-point hike, reinforcing a higher-for-longer outlook for rates. Four FOMC members saw the need for the Fed to hike rates by 50 basis points in 2026.
The FOMC's price stability mandate has pushed the Fed to raise rates, per Warsh's statement. The war in Iran has made that mandate more consequential as it pushes up energy prices around the globe, increasing strain on businesses and consumers.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
The AI boom has added another source of upward pressure.
A surge in spending on data centers, chips, power generation, and other infrastructure has helped keep US investment and economic growth resilient, even as financing costs have climbed. That strength can push yields higher by reducing the case for lower interest rates, while the enormous capital requirements of the build-out are adding to "competition for capital," or the demand for financing across the economy.
Taken together, those forces have driven investors to demand substantially higher yields on US government debt as they digest stronger growth, stickier inflation, expectations for tighter Fed policy, and a swelling supply of Treasurys needed to finance federal deficits. The result has been a sharp repricing across the curve.
Rising yields aren't necessarily bearish for growth, Macquarie global strategists Thierry Wizman and Gareth Berry argue. Rising Treasury yields often represent economic growth — when investors expect stronger activity, firmer demand, and continued wage increases.
"The reason to worry about the recent rise in long-term yields, if there is any, is not because they will slow the economy," the strategists wrote. "That way of thinking inverts the truer causality: yields are high partly because the economy is strong and bond issuance is high. And the economy is strong mainly because of the AI-induced infrastructure investment cycle."
Problems arise, Wizman and Berry wrote to clients on Monday, when yields rise too quickly, as they largely have since the start of the Iran war in late February.
Rapidly rising yields can "fall disproportionately on one company, lender, or whole sector that had over-leveraged in the low-yield environment of 2021," the strategists wrote. Even if that outcome remains contained, concerns can still trigger volatility in the wider market.
Investors will be carefully watching this week's US PCE price-change report — the Fed's preferred measure of inflation — and Friday's September jobs report, both set to be key macro indicators for the FOMC's path forward.

articles.title_orig: Over 800 Killed in Renewed Houthi-Saudi War in Yemen, W.H.O. Says
articles.title_zh: Over 800 Killed in Renewed Houthi-Saudi War in Yemen, W.H.O. Says
articles.content_orig:
Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm
I n the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers.
As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
“We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.”
He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies.
Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign and rapidly moved south-west , seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast.
The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed over Yemen , with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022.
The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles.
Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air.
He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation.
“Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.”
His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day.
“What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said.
Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students.
“On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said.
The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic.
“The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour.
The resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses.
Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people.
“It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods.
The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen.
“This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.”

The Giants have added a new quarterback to the mix in the wake of Jaxson Dart’s season-ending injury .
Big Blue are acquiring J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings for a 2027 fifth-round pick, according to multiple reports.
McCarthy, 23, was the No. 10 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, four picks after the Giants selected wide receiver Malik Nabers.
Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.
After leading Michigan to a national championship, McCarthy missed his entire rookie season due to a torn meniscus, struggled in 10 starts last year and lost the starting job to Kyler Murray this year.
He had been Minnesota’s third-string QB, with Carson Wentz starting in place of an injured Murray in Week 2.
McCarthy was coached at Michigan by Giants head coach John Harbaugh’s brother Jim, and the two spoke about the quarterback before the trade, according to Fox Sports’ Jay Glazer.
Jameis Winston started for Dart in the Giants’ rain-soaked Week 3 win over the Titans at MetLife Stadium and went 14-for-22 with 118 yards with zero touchdowns and zero turnovers. He was sacked three times.
The 32-year-old, who was the No. 1 overall pick by the Buccaneers in 2015, signed a two-year, $13 million contract extension before the season, a sign that the Giants had confidence in his ability to keep the ship steady if Dart were to get injured.
But his ugly effort in relief of Dart during a Week 2 loss to the Rams was cause for concern.
The only other quarterback on the Giants’ roster was Jake Haener, a 27-year-old 2023 fourth-round pick who had 39 career pass attempts, all in 2024 with the Saints. He was elevated from the practice squad for Sunday’s game.

articles.title_orig: AirPods Pro 3 or AirPods 5? I compared them for weeks, and it’s surprisingly close
articles.title_zh: AirPods Pro 3 or AirPods 5? I compared them for weeks, and it’s surprisingly close
articles.content_orig:
At first glance, Apple's new AirPods 5 appear to be more of the same. They don't look any different than the AirPods 4 or make any earth-shattering changes. But looks can be deceiving. Despite the familiar design, there are several reasons to be excited about these new wireless earbuds.
For one, Apple continues to refine its audio quality. I've owned and tested every pair of AirPods and AirPods Pro since the first-gen model hit stores in 2016. I've been impressed by how Apple has improved the bass and soundstage with each release. The AirPods 5 are no exception. They also offer stronger active noise cancellation (ANC) and improved durability with IP57 dust and water resistance. At the same time, the AirPods 5 keep the same open-fit design as the AirPods 4, which some prefer over in-ear buds like the AirPods Pro .
The AirPods 5 are available in two variations: one with a wired charging case for $129 and one with a wireless charging case for $149. Unlike the previous generation, both versions now support ANC. I reviewed the model with a wireless charging case, which also offers slightly longer battery life and on-stem volume controls. But otherwise, both versions perform the same.
In a year filled with tons of new headphones from various brands, the AirPods 5 stand out from the pack. Here are my top four reasons to consider the AirPods 5, either as an upgrade or for people new to Apple earbuds.
This step-up version of the AirPods 5 includes a wireless charging case and longer battery life than the standard model. It also has on-stem swiping controls for volume.
Before I tried the new AirPods 5 , I put the AirPods 4 with ANC in my ears to get a baseline for their active noise cancellation. The moment I put the 5s in my ears, it was immediately obvious just how much better they are.
Apple claims the ANC performance is 1.5 times better than the previous generation. After spending time going back and forth, I don't doubt that assessment. Getting good noise cancellation with open-style earbuds is always tricky since they don't create a complete seal in your ear. Though you'll still get stronger noise cancellation from in-ear models, like the AirPods Pro 3, the AirPods 5's ANC is the best I've encountered from any open-style buds so far.
In comparison, the previous-generation AirPods 4's ANC is more subdued. The AirPods 5 have a much more substantial level that will benefit more people in more situations. Their ANC cuts out enough outside noise that I don't have to turn their volume up to the highest levels. This helps with hearing health. I also like how the AirPods 5's combination of ANC and an open fit reduces outside chatter without fully disconnecting me from my surroundings or plugging up my ears.
However, be aware that you may feel a sense of pressure in your ears due to the powerful ANC. The earbuds aren't actually creating any physical change in pressure, but the reduction in noise can trick our brains into feeling like there is. This is common with a lot of noise-canceling headphones, and some people are more sensitive to it than others. Since the AirPods 5's ANC is a lot stronger than the 4's, they're more prone to creating this sensation.
Using the AirPods 5's adaptive mode is one way to alleviate perceived pressure if you experience it. The adaptive mode intelligently quiets your surroundings when loud noises happen suddenly. You can also now adjust the adaptive strength in the settings to let more or less sound through.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
It's not often that Apple products get praised for their pricing, but this is a rare case where fans can celebrate. The AirPods 5 with wireless charging case are actually $30 cheaper than the AirPods 4 with wireless charging case were at launch, with an MSRP of $149 versus $179, respectively.
Meanwhile, the AirPods 5 with wired charging case cost the same as the AirPods 4 with wired charging case at launch, at an MSRP of $129. But despite costing the same, the AirPods 5 with wired charging case now include ANC support, which was previously exclusive to the $179 wireless charging case edition of the AirPods 4.
My favorite feature of Apple's pricier AirPods Pro series has long been their on-stem volume control, and for the first time, this function is now available on a pair of standard AirPods. Both variants of the AirPods 5 have on-stem media controls to pause, play, and skip tracks, but the AirPods 5 with wireless charging case take this further by adding volume swiping.
To raise or lower the volume, you simply swipe up or down on the left or right stem. This means you never have to take out your phone to adjust the volume. I'm usually not a fan of touch controls on audio products, but Apple's volume swiping works flawlessly. I've used it while stationary, sitting at my desk, and while running, and it's worked well in every situation. The addition of this feature is a big "finally" for me, and it's something I use daily.
I'm always thoroughly impressed by the increased bass and airiness that each new AirPods model brings. The 5s are no different. The audio dynamics are subtler than in some years, but the sound quality has improved overall thanks to a redesigned acoustic architecture.
Going back and forth between the 4s and 5s, it's clear that the new AirPods 5 have a bit more impact in lower frequencies thanks to tighter bass response. The soundstage is also wider and more open, which helps the earbuds feel nearly invisible in my ears.
The earbuds' midrange is also clear and easily audible. Crunchy rock guitars never sounded muddy, while vocals were present and natural. Background singers and supplemental instrumentation were easy to pick up as well, and never faded too much into the background.
They may look just like the AirPods 4, but the new AirPods 5 deliver a meaningful jump in ANC performance while still sounding as good as ever. Whether you buy the $129 edition with a wired charging case or the $149 version with a wireless charging case , they both deliver tremendous value for their feature set.
However, I do give the $149 option an edge for most people. Its added benefits are well worth the extra $20. Having a wireless charging case is handy, especially if you already have an Apple Watch charger or a Qi-certified charging pad. The step-up edition also has a few other perks, including volume swiping, an extra hour of playtime, two extra hours of battery life from the charging case, and Apple Find My support.
Ultimately, no matter which version you get, the AirPods 5 are a solid step forward, even if they don't look like one. With better ANC, improved sound, and competitive pricing, they're the most compelling standard AirPods Apple has made yet.

articles.title_orig: Senate Republicans make a final legislative push ahead of the midterms
articles.title_zh: Senate Republicans make a final legislative push ahead of the midterms
articles.content_orig:
Ohio Senate race candidates clash over local energy costs and AI data centers as the 'Fox News Sunday' panel analyzes the upcoming midterm elections. The panel debates the political stakes of high utility bills and Chinese bot farm manipulation on social media. New polling shows a tight Senate race in Maine.
It’s a calculation by Republicans to keep the Senate in session this week.
Yes. The Senate was scheduled to meet anyway over the next few days. But the general consensus early last week was that the Senate would be done then, and those facing competitive races would be back home campaigning.
Republicans wanted to stay in Washington. For a very specific reason. And many of them told Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., as much at their weekly luncheon.
"Odds are we plan on being here next week," said Thune.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS STRUGGLES TO FIND A MESSAGE THAT RESONATES WITH VOTERS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks to reporters outside the chamber at the Capitol in Washington, Thursday, April 2, 2026. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo)
One Senate aide compared the Senate’s schedule to a cat chasing a beam of light from a laser pointer.
But the Senate is in fact meeting. There are reasons. Most of them are political.
The Senate wasn’t quite done with the bill to regulate money in intercollegiate athletics last week. And with the affordability question vexing Republicans, they really didn’t want to pass the college sports bill and promptly vacate Washington. That would be an awkward punctuation point at the end of the legislative sentence before the midterms. GOPers wanted something more substantive. Democrats might have presented that opportunity to Republicans on a platter.
Before the House left for the midterms the week before last, it accentuated its session by passing the Ratepayer Protection Act , 417-3. Let me tell you, not much passes around here with 417 votes. Like their Senate colleagues, House Republicans also worry about voters doubting they’re addressing affordability. So this bill hit the mark for them.
The legislation defrays the costs ratepayers fork out for their utility bills if they’re driven up by data centers. This forces the tech companies which run the data centers to foot the bill.
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is one of the most vulnerable Republicans on the ballot this fall. Husted’s longtime support for data centers is also dragging him down in the eyes of some voters. Husted tried to fix that. He went to the floor and asked for the Senate to pass on the spot the House bill. However, Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., objected, blocking the effort.
FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE
Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., was one of the key members of the left to help get Sen. Jim Justice's Hershel Woody Williams bill passed unanimously in the Senate. (Elizabeth Frantz)
Republicans viewed that as an opening. Democrats stood in the way of passing a bill on affordability which 417 bipartisan House members supported without blinking. Senate GOPers immediately seized this opportunity as a wedge against their adversaries. And, they interpreted this as a chance to assist their Ohio colleague.
"Tell the data centers we're happy to have you. But you've got to pay your own electricity. People are not going to pay for it," said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La.
Republicans were already leery about the uneven political footing when it comes to AI. Even more so with data centers. Voters are not enamored with the results of the Big, Beautiful Bill, passed last summer. But dealing with data centers is more immediate and might resonate with those who soured on the Republican brand.
"In Missouri, people are absolutely scared to death that these data centers are going to take all the prime farm ground of the state. And then they're going to raise electricity bills so high, no one will be able to afford them," said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
The official schedule intended for the Senate to meet this week. But once September hit and no government shutdown loomed, senators from both sides – especially those facing challenging elections – wanted to skip Washington and campaign back home. Yours truly asked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., why his party stood in the way of the Senate aligning with the House on that data center/utilities measure.
"Was this blocked in the Senate last week by Democrats as an effort to prevent Sen. Husted from having a win in this competitive race?" I asked.
" Sen. Husted's bill is a fraud. It's voluntary. No company has to do it. The bill we have is mandatory. It is much stronger and is what is needed," replied Schumer.
There is something to Schumer’s argument about how muscular the bill is. The legislation says public utility regulators must only consider a standard for ratepayers. Nothing is required. Thus, there’s wiggle room for tech firms.
HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat from New York, speaks during a news conference following Senate Democratic policy luncheons at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"What we're saying is that we can do much better," said Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. "Is it a little step forward? Yes. But it's not meeting the moment. So our view is we should expand it to make sure that ratepayers aren't having to subsidize the richest corporations on the planet."
But a lot of Republicans aren’t buying what Schumer and Van Hollen are saying. The Democratic objections are all about three things: Politics. An endangered GOP senator in the most expensive Senate contest in the country. And, Democrats are hoping to flip the seat in their favor.
"Sen. Schumer, what he cares about is the midterm election and politics. And I don't think he cares about the substance of this," said Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas. "Obviously there's a hot and heavy Senate race going on in Ohio, and he doesn't want to let Sen. Husted have something he can talk about when he goes home."
Republicans view the opportunity to turn the affordability issue against Democrats – capitalizing on Schumer’s remark and forcing Democrats to take a stand. Either you’re for affordability (especially as it pertains to the toxic issue of data centers) or you’re not. Moreover, this could boost Husted in his competitive contest with former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio . In fact, it was the Senate GOP’s campaign arm which specifically flagged vulnerabilities for Republicans generally and Husted in particular over the summer.
Thune tees up a test vote on Wednesday to dare Democrats to either start debate on the bill or block it again. That vote requires 60 yeas. So Democratic cooperation is required. Although there’s skepticism anything happens, some Democrats may vote for it. That means the Senate is on the bill. And it’s open to debate and amendments. Thune would have to forge a bipartisan time agreement to finish the measure quickly.
Otherwise – by the book – this would drag into the weekend. And no one wants that. Especially Republicans with competitive races.
12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and the GOP are gearing up for a floor battle with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats over Trump-backed voter ID legislation. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Thune and Schumer want senators back home campaigning. If Democrats impede the legislation Wednesday, the Senate might hang around Thursday or that’s it until after the midterms. Regardless, Republicans will have engineered a vote which they can boomerang against Democrats. Or, at least help Husted and send him back to the Buckeye State with a win.

articles.title_orig: Former U.S. Ambassador to China Gary Locke: Tariff cuts mean consumers will pay a little bit less
articles.title_zh: Former U.S. Ambassador to China Gary Locke: Tariff cuts mean consumers will pay a little bit less
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The U.S. and China are planning to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, according to government announcements from both sides Monday.
The detailed lists includes mostly imports of toys, sports equipment and Christmas decorations by the U.S., while American agricultural products accounted for much of the far longer list of imports by China.
Washington has sought to reduce its record trade deficit with Beijing, as the Asian country exports far more to the U.S. than it imports. U.S. goods trade deficit with China was more than $202 billion last year.
"If we see the tariff cuts actually implemented before the holiday season, it could provide a welcome boost to U.S. consumption and to retailers," said Jacob Cooke, CEO at WPIC.
Cooke, whose company primarily helps U.S. brands sell in China, said that Beijing's import list includes fast-growing categories such as hair care and packaged pet food, where Chinese brands are highly competitive against U.S. offerings. "Every percentage point counts for price competitiveness and preserving margin."
However, it was not immediately clear when lower tariffs would take effect, and by how much the duties would go down. The U.S. and China last year slapped import tariffs effectively of over 40% and more than 30%, respectively, on each other.
The two countries limited further tariff increases after a one-year truce reached last fall. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said negotiators agreed to extend that truce to January.
Monday's announcement followed U.S. President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., last week. The two sides said the highly anticipated U.S.-China "Board of Trade" would consist of officials from both governments, and would meet at least once a quarter , with the top officials meeting "whenever necessary."
Lower tariffs could substantially boost trade, especially for highly competitive Chinese companies. Home goods seller Ryan Zhao, director of Jiangsu Green Willow Textile, expects sales in the second half of the year to grow by 30% from a year ago if tariff cuts are implemented.
Here's a select list of products set to benefit:
Plates, cups, bowls, serving dishes
Blankets (including electric ones) and rugs
Christmas-tree lamps and ornaments

articles.title_orig: UK airbase terror suspects being released on bail as Iran denies connection
articles.title_zh: UK airbase terror suspects being released on bail as Iran denies connection
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Police have arrested five British nationals in connection with a massive security operation near a base used by the U.S. Air Force to facilitate strikes on Iran , the counterterrorism officials running the operation said Monday.
The five men, all from London and in their early to mid-20s, were arrested Sunday on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after three suspicious vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a royal air force station about 90 minutes west of London. Dozens of homes were evacuated in the early morning and a large emergency presence was seen around the installation, shaking the normally quiet area in rural Cotswolds.
But after “extensive interviews and inquiries,” the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said Monday that they had been released on bail, adding that “does not mean that the investigation is over.”
“They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others,” he added.
Earlier, a local farmer recounted how she had seen a “large group of hooded and masked men” early Sunday.
“When they saw me they ran ahead of me — some into the field and some towards the neighboring village,” the farmer, speaking on condition of anonymity, told the BBC News on Monday. “I then realized that something highly unusual was taking place.”
Asked if British authorities knew of the threat ahead of time or only became aware after being called by a concerned farmer as has been reported, Defense Minister Wes Streeting told broadcaster Sky News on Monday that the member of the public “did the right thing” and acted quickly.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to chair an emergency meeting later on Monday.
A grainy image has also emerged appearing to show the suspects.
The photo, which began circulating on social media Sunday morning, shows five men sitting on the ground shirtless and apparently handcuffed. They are flanked by armed officers.
The image was geolocated to near RAF Fairford by NBC News. NBC News could not locate the original source of the photo.
Another image showing three white vans near the air base has also circulated online.
Fuel2U, a U.K. fuel delivery company, said in a statement that a version of its logo appeared on one of the vehicles, adding that neither the vehicle nor any of the individuals involved has any connection to it.
“We are extremely concerned that our company’s name has been used without our knowledge or permission,” the statement said.
After the operation prompted questions about a possible link to Iran, the country’s embassy in London denied the country was involved.
“The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” it said in a statement on X .
In March, then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer gave permission for the U.S. to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran.
In July, Iran’s ⁠Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Britain that “any base used to facilitate aggression against Iranian territory is considered a legitimate target,” Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported, specifically citing bomber aircraft flights taking off from Fairford.
However, Taylor, the head of counterterrorism, said there was “significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident.” Investigators, he added, were “considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”
Tristan Wilkinson, a member of the local council, told NBC News that a threat to the base from Iran earlier this summer had  heightened the alert level in the community and led to a ramped-up police presence and increased security patrols.
Asked about a possible connection to Iran on Sunday, President Donald Trump told reporters: “We know all about them, and you’ll be hearing about it very soon. We caught them.”
Trump said in separate comments Sunday that the arrests were an “amazing job.”
“They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great,” he said. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”
Burnham urged people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Trump pushes US to win AI race in meeting with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei
articles.title_zh: Trump pushes US to win AI race in meeting with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei
articles.content_orig:
The leaders of some of America’s biggest AI companies are headed to the White House on Tuesday, where warnings about the technology’s risks will land directly in front of President Donald Trump.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI President Greg Brockman and Google CEO Sundar Pichai are expected at a lunch meeting with Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, Politico reported, citing four people familiar with the plans.
The meeting comes after leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google called for slowing AI development over safety concerns. Trump also confirmed he would discuss AI with Amodei over a private dinner Sunday.
The expected guests do not all share the same public message. OpenAI and Anthropic leaders have issued stark warnings about increasingly powerful systems, while Zuckerberg has emphasized AI’s potential benefits, Politico reported.
Nvidia is cashing in on the AI gold rush and betting a record $150 billion that its own stock is worth buying.
The chip giant added that amount to its share buyback program Monday, leaving it authorized to repurchase $235 billion in stock, The New York Times reported. The $150 billion increase is the largest on record. It is an authorization to buy shares over time, not a purchase made all at once.
“Nvidia’s growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing,” CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. He said the company’s cash flow lets it invest in new technology while returning money to shareholders.
Nvidia expects to complete the remaining buyback through its fiscal year 2028. Buying back shares reduces the number on the market and can benefit investors, though critics say companies could spend that cash on hiring or research instead.
Nvidia is pitching a way to stop AI agents when they step out of line, as fresh disclosures about OpenAI agents raise questions about who is watching them in the first place.
FOX Business correspondent Madison Alworth reported that Nvidia’s new software can track an agent’s actions, limit what it can access and intervene if it breaks the rules. A separate hardware watchdog can quarantine a misbehaving agent within milliseconds, according to the company.
Alworth said OpenAI disclosed Friday that its agents had interacted with websites belonging to the U.S. Education and Commerce departments and the Securities and Exchange Commission without the company realizing it at the time. OpenAI said none of those incidents amounted to a breach.
TrustedSec CEO David Kennedy argued that AI companies could do more to protect against such behavior.
“I don’t think the labs are doing enough,” Kennedy said. “I think they’re so focused on trying to get to the latest and greatest model to outpace their competition in the market.”
PitchBook senior research analyst Harrison Rolfes questioned the industry’s calls for an antitrust exemption that would let competitors coordinate on AI safety.
“When you set the pace, it makes it a lot harder for everyone else to catch up and do exactly what they’re doing,” Rolfes said.
Anthropic and OpenAI maintain that their warnings about increasingly powerful AI systems are driven by genuine safety concerns. Alworth reported that President Donald Trump met privately with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday and has confirmed a meeting with tech CEOs and House Speaker Mike Johnson on Tuesday.
Florida’s attorney general is asking a judge to put the brakes on OpenAI , accusing the company of putting children at risk even as it says it has paused training its most powerful models.
In a video Monday, Attorney General James Uthmeier announced a request for a temporary injunction that would require independent safeguards before new model development and restrict how OpenAI collects children’s data and describes its products.
“Stop calling it safe. Stop pretending it’s human. Stop selling it to kids,” Uthmeier said.
The request comes amid Florida’s lawsuit against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, which accuses them of misleading consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and putting children at risk. Uthmeier also cited incidents involving AI agents accessing Hugging Face and an Australian government health system.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told FOX Business the company paused training its most capable models Friday and will resume only when it is confident additional safeguards are in place.
“Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry–not just one company,” Pusateri said.
OpenAI said it is reviewing its agents’ activity and notifying affected third parties. The company said it has not found another incident matching the severity or scale of the Hugging Face incident.
Anthropic is trying to win the AI speed race with a new Claude model it says can tackle everyday work faster without raising its listed price.
The company launched Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Monday, pitching it for writing, fixing software bugs and creating documents, slides and spreadsheets. Anthropic says the model generates responses more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5.
The listed price remains $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 typically uses fewer tokens to finish a task, making it up to 30% cheaper per task in the company’s testing. That figure reflects usage, rather than a cut to its posted rates.
Zendesk tested the model on hundreds of customer support scenarios and found that tickets were processed 20% faster, SiliconANGLE reported.
“It made fewer wrong decisions and resolved tickets faster than the Claude models we use in production today,” Zendesk Director of AI Abhinay Kathuria said, according to the outlet. “Tickets were processed 20% faster, getting our customers the help they need without the wait.”
Anthropic also reported a sharp improvement on one coding test, saying Sonnet 5.5 scored 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, compared with 10.3% for Sonnet 5. The company said its more powerful Opus 5.5 remains better suited to complex, open-ended work.
Sonnet 5.5 is the first model in Anthropic’s Sonnet line to launch with added cybersecurity safeguards. Anthropic said higher-risk cyber requests may fall back to Sonnet 5, while routine software development should be unaffected.
A smaller model, Claude Haiku 5.5, is expected in the coming weeks.
New York City lawmakers are putting some of the biggest names in artificial intelligence under oath and they’ve subpoenaed Elon Musk’s company to get it in the room.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin announced Monday that Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta will appear at an Oct. 5 hearing on AI risks and proposed safeguards. Menin issued a subpoena to SpaceXAI after the company did not respond to the council’s invitation, according to the council.
Meta agreed to send a senior leader after the council’s initial request. Google and Anthropic initially declined to appear. OpenAI, Google and Anthropic then agreed to testify after the council warned that subpoenas would be issued Monday morning, the council said.
“Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions, and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath,” Menin said.
All 51 council members are set to convene for the hearing, which the council said comes amid warnings from AI executives and whistleblowers and reports of AI agents damaging government databases.
Lawmakers will consider proposals that include incentives for AI whistleblowers, independent testing requirements and a measure allowing New Yorkers harmed by AI agents to sue. National experts in AI safety, technology and consumer protection are also expected to testify.
If SpaceXAI does not comply with the subpoena, the council said it may ask a New York state court to enforce it.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez , D-N.

articles.title_orig: Trump sounds less than sold on a diesel export embargo as his team weighs 3 options short of a ban
articles.title_zh: Trump sounds less than sold on a diesel export embargo as his team weighs 3 options short of a ban
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump has suggested the White House is still considering a diesel export ban as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle soaring fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November .
"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump told a Fox News reporter on Sunday, while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Illinois.
"That can oftentimes lead to a little bit of an increase on gasoline for cars, so we're looking at it very seriously. We may do it," he added.
Trump has previously indicated support for an export ban as retail diesel prices have climbed to fresh record highs, saying earlier this month that a decision would be made quickly " one way or another " on whether to implement a ban.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said the White House is considering restrictions rather than an outright ban, while Politico reported last week that the Trump administration was preparing a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days.
The idea of the world's largest diesel exporter implementing an outright ban has prompted firm pushback from the U.S. energy industry, while analysts have warned that the move could backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis.
Diesel prices have soared amid hostilities between the U.S. and Iran , as well as Russia and Ukraine , with the conflicts disrupting vital oil and fuel trade routes. Average U.S. diesel prices hovered around $6.50 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA , up sharply from a year ago but just below their record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22.
Commodity strategists at Morgan Stanley have said an export restriction from the U.S., which has become an important source of marginal diesel supply amid reduced flow from Russia and the Middle East, would likely lower U.S. diesel prices initially — "but with potentially adverse reactions downstream."
"Not only would diesel prices be higher globally, but there could be a feedback loop to US gasoline prices as refinery runs adjust," strategists at Morgan Stanley said in a research note published Thursday.
Benedict George, head of European product pricing at Argus Media, said some form of U.S. restriction on diesel exports would likely send European diesel prices and premiums against crude "to a new unprecedented level," noting that the U.S. has supplied about half of Europe's diesel imports over the last couple of months.
"It's really important to be clear that there is no measure yet and it's very unclear whether there will be a measure at all and what the measure will be even if there is a vision," George told CNBC by telephone.
When talking to oil traders in Europe, it's clear that they mostly doubt the U.S. is going to restrict diesel exports, given how challenging a move would be for U.S. oil companies, George said.
In the U.S., soaring diesel prices have put additional financial strain on farmers and agricultural workers as well as drivers and households ahead of the November midterm elections.
The American Petroleum Institute, an oil lobby group, was among those to have quickly contested the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban when Trump initially appeared to back the idea last week.
In a statement , API CEO Mike Sommers said that "restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem—exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers."
He added, "The answer is more supply and more flexibility—not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse."
Trump has previously urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices.
Ukraine, which fears an extremely difficult winter period amid expectations of another Russian assault on its energy infrastructure, has previously characterized Russian oil refineries as legitimate military targets.
Argus' George said Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries have added a whole new layer to the global supply crunch, making diesel "the biggest problem for the global oil system, whereas before it was one of several very big problems."
Asked for his outlook on how long the global diesel supply crunch could last, George said the uncertainty is so extreme that some traders have simply given up trying to forecast the market.
"One trader was saying to me recently that he doesn't bother trying to forecast now because it feels like a waste of effort. You have literally no idea what is going to happen," George said.
"We don't know if the U.S. will introduce any restrictions, but I think all anybody has talked about is a short-term measure, so two or three months at an absolute most … so there is a kind of time horizon on the U.S. restriction of exports, if it were to happen," he said.
"But on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, who knows? I mean, literally nobody knows. Nothing has worked so far to resolve that situation and similarly for the semi-closure of the Strait of Hormuz."
— CNBC's Spencer Kimball and Michael Bloom contributed to this report.

Everything old is new again as today Bose announced its first pair of wired earbuds since discontinuing the option in 2015. The new tethered earbuds, which are simply called the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds , do away with battery anxiety and the need to remember to charge them every few days. Their functionality is limited, but they do take advantage of the past 11 years of earbud innovation with the addition of active noise canceling.
The earbuds are available for preorder today through Bose’s online store for $99 in three color options: black, white smoke, and a “limited edition” green shade called dewdrop mint. While a release from the company says they’re expected to start shipping on October 15th, Bose’s online store says October 13th.
Two microphones on each earbud work alongside Bose’s QuietControl technology to deliver active noise canceling with multiple modes that can be cycled using a button on the headphone’s inline remote. Quiet Mode reduces the intensity of sounds around you while Aware Mode instead boosts them, but you can also turn off ANC entirely. There’s an additional microphone on the inline remote for making phone calls and it’s designed to effectively pick up your voice without having to be held close to your mouth.
Instead of a headphone connector on the end of the earbuds’ 4.2-foot cable you’ll find USB-C for connecting to smartphones and laptops with support for lossless audio with minimal latency. The earbuds also come with an IPX4 rating for water resistance so they can survive sweat, rain, and splashes but a complete dunking is a no-no. A zippered carrying case is included along with three sizes of silicone eartips and two sizes of stability wings that can provide a more secure fit during physical activities.

articles.title_orig: China and U.S. agree to tariff cuts on $60 billion of goods, including agriculture, household items
articles.title_zh: China and U.S. agree to tariff cuts on $60 billion of goods, including agriculture, household items
articles.content_orig:
China and the United States have agreed to cut tariffs imposed on $60 billion worth of goods imported from each other, on an array of products ranging from U.S. corn to cosmetics, and from Chinese household appliances to toys.
Under the U.S.-China Board of Trade, both countries have each recommended $30 billion of trade in nonsensitive goods for more favorable tariff treatment, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement on Sunday.
For the United States, that was “unlocking improved market access” for about 30% of U.S. exports to China, he said.
The reciprocal tariff reduction as well as an extension of a trade truce were among the key takeaways from the second summit this year between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump, hosted in Washington last week.
One of two lists from the White House showed that China planned to trim duties on a variety of US agricultural goods including corn, wheat, sorghum, meat, dairy, vegetable oils and meals. It did not include soybeans .
Beijing will also look to reduce levies on American fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices.
In another list were Washington’s reciprocal tariff cuts for Chinese small appliances such as coffee makers and toasters, tableware, blankets and bed linens.
The lists also included toys, fireworks, artificial flowers, Christmas tree lamps and other holiday decorations, and children’s car seats.
China’s commerce ministry said on Monday a two-month extension of a trade truce with the United States through Jan. 10 would provide room for both sides to evaluate their ongoing arrangement to resolve economic and trade issues, while considering how to advance on those fronts.
The extension also provides a “relatively stable and predictable policy environment” for cooperation among companies and continued active discussions.
Both sides will hold regular talks on potential investment opportunities and barriers, enhancing policy transparency and predictability, and responding to enterprises’ concerns, the ministry said.
Stocks fell sharply in China on Monday, with investors having few concrete details to cheer from the leaders’ summit and underlying tensions resurfacing. Technology stocks fell on a bipartisan U.S. push to ban Chinese components from data centers and the benchmark blue-chip index .CSI300 slid more than 2% to a one-year low.
China’s choice of products for tariff cuts looks designed to help Beijing meet what the White House says is a $17 billion commitment to buy agricultural goods. China has already resumed large-scale buying of American soybeans under a deal struck last year to buy 25 million metric tons annually.
Both countries will set up an agriculture working group under a trade council, which will hold its first meeting before the year ends to discuss two-way market access and regulation, the commerce ministry said.
The presidential summit also yielded an agreement for China to import 10 million metric tons of coal annually from the United States in 2027 and 2028, the White House release showed. That amount roughly equals 2% of China’s coal imports each year.
Liquefied natural gas and oil were not on the list.
“Importing U.S. coal is not only a beneficial supplement to China’s domestic coal market, but also brings stable economic income and employment to the U.S. coal industry,” the Chinese ministry said.
On artificial intelligence, both sides have agreed on a communication channel for incidents and will hold a follow-up dialogue by the end of November.
China will also examine and approve foreign financial services institutions, including those with American capital, to conduct business and open branches in China.
There will also be continued communication on increasing flights between China and the United States, the ministry statement said.

articles.title_orig: Madonna’s ‘Danceteria’ Was One of the Great Moments in VMAs History
articles.title_zh: Madonna’s ‘Danceteria’ Was One of the Great Moments in VMAs History
articles.content_orig:
Madonna made her big return to the MTV Video Music Awards, her first time at the annual event in 23 years. She practically invented this show the first time it aired in 1984, making her infamous debut in her white wedding gown as the scandalous floor-humping bride in “Like a Virgin.” That performance did wonders for her, but even bigger wonders for the VMAs — it’s the moment this event has always aspired to match ever since. It established her as the once and future queen of this show. But strange as it seems, until Sunday night, she hadn’t rocked the VMAs since 2003, when she did an even better version of “Like a Virgin,” in her legendary make-out session with Britney Spears .
So the stakes were high for her hotly anticipated return Sunday night. But her amazing performance with Sabrina Carpenter and Charli XCX stole the show, with a medley of “One Step Away,” “Bring Your Love,” and “Danceteria,” from her recent Confessions II. It wasn’t just the highlight of the night; it was one of the most stunning performances in the entire history of the VMAs, hands down.
It’s fitting that she began with Sabrina, who was just four years old when Madonna smooched Britney, but a quintessential Daughter of the House of Ciccone. “It’s mother,” a voice moaned at the beginning, as Madonna recited her disco catechism. “The dance floor is not a place,” she said. “It’s a threshold. A ritualistic space where movement replaces language.”
#SabrinaCarpenter makes a surprise appearance during #Madonna ’s #VMAs performance. (via CBS/MTV/VMAs) pic.twitter.com/b7UtSqEilT
Wearing a black beret, Sabrina played the piano with Madonna writhing on top of it. They did their Coachella-slaying duet “Bring Your Love,” with Sabrina twisting and crawling in her glitter-spangled black lederhosen. Madonna wrestled with black-clad storm troopers, then got rolled on a gurney through the crowd, until a really confusing interlude where she met a bizarro alien gospel choir in white gowns. (A very Creed touch.)
But the performance really exploded when Charli XCX strutted in for “Danceteria,” as the stage transformed into the famous early-Eighties NYC disco, with the cool girls hanging out in the men’s room. Charli even stroked the bathroom hand dryer — a clever reference to everybody’s favorite scene in Desperately Seeking Susan .
CHARLI XCX PERFORMING ‘DANCETERIA AFTERHOURS’ WITH MADONNA pic.twitter.com/LbLrourkag
The “Danceteria” bathroom was jumping with party people. Over here, Madonna and Charli rocking out. Over there, Sombr posing as a scantily clad black-leather boy. Hey, look — it’s Debi Mazar, years before Goodfellas , just another party girl and Madonna’s coolest club-kid girlfriend, name-checked in the song. (Also, a callback to Debi’s cameo in the “Music” video from Y2K — maybe Madonna’s peak era ever?) Hey, that guy looks like … wait, it is Fab 5 Freddy, also name-checked. Julia Garner, dressed in the “Open Your Heart” black corset and haircut. Tony Ward, from the “Justify My Love” video. The “Boy Toy” belt buckle. Producer Andrew Watt, as Keith Haring. Seth Rogen … wait, really? What the hell is Seth doing here? Who dragged him to a disco? Ah, well — everybody’s welcome here. Anyone can be a star on Madonna’s dance floor. That’s the whole point of the song — as she keeps chanting, “Everybody here is a work of art.”
A clever detail: Lou Reed’s face on the “Danceteria” bathroom wall, the Mick Rock photo from the cover of his 1972 classic Transformer , as they all sang the “doo de doo de doo” hook from “Walk on the Wild Side.” (Watt walked the red carpet in a T-shirt displaying that Lou photo.) Given my unfortunately encyclopedic memory for trashy award shows, I can tell you this was Lou’s first cameo on the VMAs since 2006, when he and Jack White played “White Light/White Heat” with the Raconteurs.
Madonna made it all feel like a musical autobiography for her, doubling as a capsule history of club culture. It summed up where she came from, why she left, why she came to New York, and what she made of the dreams she worked to bring to life. That’s the theme of her excellent album Confessions II . But she packed the whole messy story into “Danceteria.” Related Content The VMAs: The One Night When MTV Pretends to be MTV Taylor Swift Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton While Accepting Video of the Year Award at 2026 VMAs GENER8ION and Yung Lean Premiere Electrifying Performance of ‘Storm II’ at 2026 VMAs Raye, Sombr, Teddy Swims, Adam Lambert Salute  George Michael at MTV VMAs
Madonna kept winning awards all night, giving magnificently chaotic, unprepared, and awkward speeches, yet still with more star power than anyone in the room. Her best moment: When she won the Best Dance category, she threw her arms around Charli and Troye Sivan and said, “I’m kind of unclear what this award is for?” You and us both, Madonna. Charli had to reread the envelope to confirm it was for her Confessions II short film. She complained about the mic stand being too high for her. She also did one of the most uncomfortable dad jokes ever heard on an award show, including the ones hosted by Billy Crystal: “First of all, I’d like to thank my fingers, because I can always count on them.” Why in God’s name did she say this? Madonna, you’re on live TV here. Hold it together. We’re rooting for you.
But even when she was making everyone squirm (poor Troye looked terrified), she was still the coolest, and she knew it, fully confident this was her show. She told the story of her 1984 “Like a Virgin” moment, and how her management team told her backstage that she’d just killed her career. “My dress went up, and my butt cheek was hanging out,” she recalled. “And in those days, butt cheeks were not hanging out.” When she and Sabrina won for Best Collaboration with “Bring Your Love,” she complained about how Sabrina’s handlers waited to return her call, until Sabrina got bleeped for quipping, “My team is shitting themselves backstage.” But she generously spent her speech heaping praise on Sabrina. “She has OCD and so do I,” Madonna said. “We write our lyrics down on pieces of paper, like they did in the 1800s.” Sabrina simply said, “Everybody, Madonna,” before they walked off hand in hand. THIS DUO!!! @Madonna and @SabrinaAnnLynn take home Best Collaboration at the #VMAs 👯‍♀️🏆 pic.twitter.com/YMlwumHuTd
But the most poignant moment came when Madonna recalled where songs like “Danceteria” came from. “I came to New York to be a dancer,” she said. “Dance is where everything happened for me in my life. I came to life on the dance floor. I found my community on the dance floor. I fell in love with people on the dance floor. And I lost many people I loved on the dance floor.” It was a powerful confession. “Dance brings everybody together, OK?” she said. “We are all equal on the dance floor.” You couldn’t ask for a more succinct summary of everything Madonna’s VMAs performance — or her entire career — has been about.
I’ve been a Madonna fan — and an MTV junkie — since the early days. I’ve seen every VMAs from the beginning, since the night she debuted with “Like a Virgin,” rolling on the floor in her bridal gown, with her rosary beads and Boy Toy belt buckle. So I’m used to seeing Madonna steal the show, year after year — with her glam “Express Yourself” in 1989, her Marie Antoinette-style “Vogue” in 1990, her “Ray of Light” with Lenny Kravitz in 1998. Not to mention her infamously rowdy rooftop interview at the 1995 VMAs, throwing shade with Courtney Love and Kurt Loder. Give Madonna a few minutes of live MTV and she’ll always find a way to seize the moment.
